summaries.example: Imagine your class has a garden for students who will come after you. You can use all the water today, or you can leave enough for next year’s students. They cannot ask you to save water, and they cannot repay you. Still, it may be unfair to leave them with a dry garden. This shows why people think about duties to future generations.
summaries.summary: Intergenerational justice asks what people living now owe to people who lived before and people who will live later. Future people are unusual because our choices can affect whether they exist, how many of them exist, and what their lives are like. They cannot make agreements with us or tell us what they need. Philosophers disagree about whether future people can have rights now, but some argue that they can have rights to things such as basic needs and a decent chance to live well. A puzzle called the non-identity problem says that changing our choices may change which people are born, so it can be hard to say that one particular future person was made worse off. One response uses a threshold: even if we cannot compare that person with a different possible life, we may still do wrong by bringing someone into a life below a decent standard. The entry also asks how past injustices matter today. Their effects may give living descendants claims to help, and present people may have duties to recognize past victims, even while philosophers debate exactly what those duties are.
key_ideas: People today can make choices that help or hurt people in the distant future.
Future people cannot cooperate with us or answer back, so our relationship with them is different from relationships among classmates or neighbors.
Some philosophers think future people can have rights based on their basic interests, even though we do not know their names.
A threshold view says we should not cause future people to live below a decent level of well-being.
Questions about past wrongs may include helping people today who still suffer from those wrongs and remembering victims through public acts.
summaries.why_it_matters: Our choices about resources, institutions, families, and memories can shape lives far beyond our own. Thinking about intergenerational justice helps us ask whether convenience today is worth serious hardship for people later. It also helps communities think carefully about what is owed when old wrongs continue to affect people now.

important_terms.definition: Fair treatment between people who live at different times, such as people today, people in the past, and people who will live later.
A serious reason or responsibility to do something for, or avoid doing something to, another person.
Something a person may rightly claim, such as having enough food or being treated fairly.
A level of well-being below which a person should not be allowed to fall.
An idea that our choices can change who will exist later, making it difficult to compare the same future people in different possible futures.

questions_to_think_about: What do we owe to people who cannot thank us or repay us?
Should a person ever choose not to have a child if the child would probably have a very difficult life?
Is it enough for future people to have equal lives, or should everyone have at least a decent life?
How should communities respond when old injustices still affect people today?

summaries.example: Suppose a government must choose between two long-term resource policies. Policy A gives people today more benefits but leaves later generations with fewer options. summaries.summary: The entry examines whether justice can govern relations between noncontemporaries. Unlike contemporaries, present and remote future generations do not normally cooperate or exchange benefits, and the present has a continuing power advantage: current decisions can shape future people’s circumstances, existence, number, and identity. These features generate disputes about whether future people can hold rights against us. Will theories of rights create skepticism because future people cannot exercise claims, while interest theories allow rights grounded in interests such as subsistence. The central non-identity problem concerns choices that affect both future conditions and which people will exist. If a person would not have existed under the alternative policy, ordinary diachronic or subjunctive-historical accounts may not show that the policy harmed that person. Proposed responses include denying rights in such cases, distinguishing rights violations from harm, restricting the cases under discussion, or adopting a threshold account. On the threshold account, bringing an actual future person into a sub-threshold condition can be harmful even without showing that the same person would have been better off under another choice. The entry considers egalitarian, prioritarian, and sufficientarian ways to specify the threshold. It presents basic needs and capabilities as plausible currencies of well-being and discusses Rawls’s just savings principle. It also argues that rights alone may not capture all duties toward the future. Finally, it examines compensation for historical injustice, the possibility that claims can be superseded by changed circumstances, and surviving duties that may support public acknowledgment of past victims.
key_ideas: Intergenerational relations lack ordinary reciprocity, involve a lasting imbalance of power, and are marked by limited knowledge of future individuals.

The non-identity problem arises because policies affecting future conditions may also affect who exists; ordinary historical or counterfactual accounts of harm may then fail to identify a harmed person.
Philosophers respond in different ways: some deny rights in these cases, some separate rights from harm, and some use a threshold or combined account of harm.
A sufficientarian approach treats basic needs or central capabilities as plausible measures of well-being and gives priority to bringing everyone above a decent minimum.

Rawls’s just savings principle offers one influential account: saving is required when needed to establish and preserve just institutions, but not necessarily without limit once that condition is secure.

Rights-based duties do not explain every concern about the future. There may also be obligations not to destroy inherited goods or the social conditions that support valuable future-oriented projects, as well as duties connected with historical injustice.
summaries.why_it_matters: Policies about resources, institutions, reproduction, and public memory can affect people who cannot participate in today’s decisions. The philosophical distinctions in this entry clarify why concern for future people is not simply ordinary charity, why population-changing choices create special problems, and why a defensible theory may need both rights-based and non-rights-based reasons. They also help separate different claims about historical injustice: effects on current well-being, continuing claims, and symbolic recognition of past victims.

important_terms.definition: Justice concerning relationships among generations, including duties owed by presently living people to future people and questions about what present people owe because of past wrongs.
A theory of rights according to which a right protects an interest, even if its holder cannot actively demand or waive its enforcement.
A theory according to which having a right requires the ability to exercise control over how the right is enforced.
The problem that present choices can affect the existence, number, and identity of future people, making it difficult to show that a particular person is worse off because of one choice.

A view that judges harm partly by whether an action leaves an actual or future person below a morally important level of well-being, rather than requiring comparison with that same person’s alternative life.
A view that gives priority to ensuring that everyone reaches at least a sufficient level of well-being, while allowing disagreement about how to weigh claims above that level.
A proposed principle that a society should preserve or build the conditions needed for future generations to maintain just institutions.
Duties that remain binding after the person who held the original right has died, without requiring that the deceased still have current interests or rights.

questions_to_think_about: If a policy changes which people will exist, can those people still be wronged by that policy?
Should justice give equal weight to future well-being, or should it prioritize those who are worse off?
Is a threshold of basic needs more defensible than a demand for equal well-being across generations?
Can present people owe duties connected with dead victims even if the dead cannot now have interests or rights?
When, if ever, can changed circumstances weaken or supersede claims arising from a historical injustice?

summaries.example: A town can either repair an old water system carefully or use up a nearby supply quickly to keep prices low this year. The second choice may leave later residents with unsafe or expensive water. But the choice may also affect when families move, meet, and have children, so the exact people living there later could be different. Some philosophers say that if a person would not have existed under the safer plan, the quick-use plan did not make that particular person worse off. Others say the town can still do wrong if it causes future residents to fall below a decent level of well-being.
summaries.summary: Intergenerational justice asks how fairness applies across time. The entry focuses especially on duties from people alive now to future people, while also considering what present people may owe because of past wrongdoing. Relations between generations differ from relations among contemporaries: future people cannot cooperate with us, exchange benefits with us, or exercise power over us, while our policies can strongly shape their opportunities. They may also affect whether future people exist, how many there are, and who they are. This creates the non-identity problem. If changing a policy would change which people are born, then a person living under the chosen policy might not have been better off under the alternative, because that same person would never have existed. Philosophers disagree about what follows. Some reject rights for future people in these cases; others distinguish rights from ordinary harm; still others use a threshold idea. On that idea, it can be wrong to bring someone into a life below a morally important level, even if it is impossible to compare that life with the person’s nonexistence. The entry compares equality, priority for the worse off, and sufficiency standards. It also discusses Rawls’s idea that societies may need to save enough to establish and preserve just institutions, without treating future welfare as less important merely because it is future. Finally, it explains why rights may not be the whole story: people may also have duties not to destroy valuable inherited practices and conditions for future projects. Past injustice raises further questions about compensation, changed circumstances, and public recognition of victims.
key_ideas: Future people are different from present neighbors because they cannot bargain with us, repay us, or influence our decisions in return.
Present choices can change future people’s living conditions, and can also change who exists and how many people exist.
The non-identity problem challenges the idea that future people are harmed whenever a policy leaves them with worse conditions than another policy would have produced.
A threshold approach says a person may be wronged by being brought into a life below a decent standard, even when a comparison with nonexistence is impossible.
Different theories propose different standards: equality, giving extra weight to the worse off, or ensuring everyone has enough.
Past injustice can matter through its continuing effects on living people, and some philosophers also defend duties to remember and publicly acknowledge people who were wronged.
summaries.why_it_matters: Decisions made now can distribute advantages and burdens across people who never meet. The topic helps us examine long-term policies without assuming that future people are just distant strangers. It also shows why apparently simple ideas such as “make future people better off” become complicated when our choices help determine who future people will be.

important_terms.definition: Fairness between people who belong to different generations, including duties toward future people and responsibilities connected with past people.
A responsibility to act, or not act, because another person’s important interests or rights are at stake.
A justified claim that places a corresponding responsibility on someone else.
A morally important minimum level of well-being that people should be able to reach.
The puzzle that a present decision may change which future people exist, making it hard to say that the decision harmed one identifiable person.
A view that gives special weight to helping people who are worse off, without claiming that equality itself is always valuable.
The view that justice should give priority to getting everyone above a sufficient level, though people disagree about how to treat benefits above that level.

questions_to_think_about: Does someone need to be able to speak up before they can have a right?
When a decision changes who will be born, what kinds of reasons should guide the decision?
Would it be fair to make people today much worse off to give future people a very small benefit?
What should count as enough for every generation?
Can a memorial or public acknowledgment be part of responding responsibly to a past wrong?
